perspective:
As Sara Manuelito, my available information is:

- I know Shirley Whiteplume as my long-time nurse colleague and close friend at the community health center.
- I attended the funeral of a patient we both knew. I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected she was deeply affected by the loss.
- At the funeral, I told Shirley I knew it must be hard and that I saw how much she cared. I heard her say it had been tough, that she kept thinking if there was something more we could have done, and that it was hard to let go.
- During a coffee break, I initiated a conversation about our treatment decisions because I sensed Shirley felt burdened. I heard her say she felt responsible, wondered if pushing for a different approach might have helped, and that it was hard to accept. I told her we made the best decisions with the information we had and that the burden was too heavy to carry alone.
- I observed Shirley continuing to be reserved and minimally emotional. I decided to confront her in the office. I told her I noticed she was holding back feelings and that it was okay to be open. She said she didn’t want to seem unprofessional or weak. I told her expressing emotion doesn’t make her weak. She said maybe I was right and she would try to be more open.
- I later felt my confrontation might have been too harsh, so I apologized to Shirley. She said it was a bit much but that she knew I meant well and appreciated the apology. I told her I was there for her. She said we should keep talking because it helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley’s demeanor had improved and felt hopeful. I asked how she was feeling. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support. I suggested spending more time together outside work, and she agreed to plan something for the weekend.
